text.p: Shareholders in Shell Transport & Trading Plc, the British arm of the Anglo-Dutch group, on Wednesday rejected a hotly- disputed resolution aimed at beefing up Shell's human rights and environmental policies.

The exact outcome of the vote was not immediately available, but chairman John Jennings told the annual meeting, which saw activists demonstrate outside and inside. he had cast 316 million shares by proxy against the resolution compared with 357 million shares in total.
Shell had urged shareholders to vote against the resolution, which was seconded by shareholder action group, Pirc.

John Hall, a clergyman from the ecumenical council for corporate responsibility, which cooperated with Pirc on the resolution, had said before the vote he did not expect it to be adopted, and its defeat was widely expected.

The resolution called for an independent audit of Shell's human rights and environmental policies, which the resolution's backers said would lead to greater transparency and prevent misinformation from either the company or its critics.
Shell released its own worldwide health, safety and environment report last week. Rebel shareholders said the company was moving forward but still saw a need for an independent assessment.
"Environmental matters are at the heart of its (Shell's) commercial future," said Anne Simpson of Pirc.
About 40 activists, including representatives of Friends of the Earth and Nigeria's Ogoniland region, had gathered outside the meeting, beating drums and chanting "People not profits."
There were no signs of violence and security was tight.
The Royal Dutch/Shell Group has come under increasing pressure from activists who accuse the company of harming the environment and supporting Nigeria's military rulers.
The company has dismissed such criticism, arguing that it has reduced emissions of greenhouse gases and is committed to human rights.
